item.research_question: How does the machinability of Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy compare to 304 stainless steel in terms of cutting forces, tool wear, surface quality, and microstructural changes during milling?
item.material_system: Al0.6CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA) and X5CrNi18-10 (304) stainless steel
item.processing_route: Face milling using a 12 mm diameter shank cutter with two indexable carbide inserts (grade HSC 05, PVTi coating) on a FIRST MCV 300 vertical milling center; dry cutting conditions; 25 tests using Taguchi method with cutting speed (vc), feed per tooth (fz), and axial depth of cut (ap) varied; radial depth of cut ae = 12 mm (100%); sample dimensions 145 × 15 × 6 mm³ for HEA
item.test_conditions: Dry cutting; spindle speeds up to 8000 rpm; feed rates up to 103 mm/min; axial depth of cut (ap) ranging from 0.1 mm to 0.42 mm; feed per tooth (fz) ranging from 0.05 mm/tooth to 0.15 mm/tooth; cutting speed (vc) varied across 5 levels; temperature measured via thermo vision camera (0–500 °C range); cutting forces measured with Kistler 9257B dynamometer
key_findings: The machinability of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of 304 stainless steel based on the resultant cutting force.
Cutting temperatures ranged from 120 °C to 281 °C, with the maximum temperature (213.2 °C) recorded after about 6 s of processing.
The axial depth of cut (ap) was identified as the main influencing parameter on cutting temperature, with maximum temperatures (240–281 °C) occurring at ap = 0.42 mm.
Maximum flank wear width (VBB max) was 86 µm for the first cutting edge (CE1) and 67 µm for the second cutting edge (CE2).
Maximum crater dimensions on the rack face for CE2 were KBmax = 490 µm and KMmax = 225 µm.
Surface roughness values ranged from 0.39 µm to 2.058 µm, with the best values obtained at minimum feed (fz = 0.05 mm/tooth).
Microhardness of the machined HEA surfaces ranged from 365 HV0.2 to 444 HV0.2, attributed to material inhomogeneity and self-hardening.
XRD analysis showed that patterns for as-cast and machined surfaces were very similar, with no new phases formed during machining.
item.mechanism: The superior machinability of the HEA compared to stainless steel is attributed to its specific cutting force behavior, where the resultant force is lower despite higher hardness. The irregular chip fragmentation and surface defects are caused by the inhomogeneity of the cast material and the presence of hard intermetallic phases (e.g., Fe2Al5, FeAl3) which act as micro-edges causing tool wear. Self-hardening effects and oxidation during cutting contribute to the increased microhardness and chip fragmentation, while the similar XRD patterns indicate the material withstands heating cycles without phase transformation.
item.limitations: The study was limited to dry cutting conditions and did not evaluate the effects of cooling and lubrication. The research is described as preliminary, and the number of reference XRD patterns available in the database is limited. The study did not cover extended ranges of cutting parameters for finish and rough cuts, nor did it generate predictive mathematical models for material removal rate or tool life.
item.future_work: More detailed research should be achieved to have a more precise image of the machinability of the HEA by considering the cutting speed, material removal rate and cutting tool life. Furthermore, extended ranges of the cutting parameters should be considered for both finish cut and rough cut and to generate predictive mathematical models to improve processing and optimize cutting parameters.
quotes: In terms of cutting forces, the behavior of the HEA was found to be about 59% better than that of stainless steel.
The maximum value of temperature reached after about 6 s of processing is Tmax = 213.2 °C.

Preliminary cutting tests showed that conventional cutting tool materials, such as rapid steel, have very limited life and suffer an abrasion wear process resulting in a large amount of heat in the cutting process.
